topic: Introduction to Health Insurance and the Health System in India
t: The National Health Mission (NHM) of the Government of India was formed in 2013 by bringing together:
o: CGHS and ESIS
PM-JAY and RSBY
The National Rural Health Mission and the National Urban Health Mission
AYUSH and allopathic services
e: NRHM (2005) and NUHM (2013) were subsumed under NHM to strengthen public health delivery; PM-JAY is a separate financing scheme.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: Under the 'National Health Insurance' (single-payer) model, as in Canada:
o: The government both finances and directly provides all care through public hospitals
A single public insurer pays for care delivered largely by private providers
Employers must set up their own sickness funds
Patients pay providers directly and claim nothing
e: The single-payer model separates financing (public) from provision (mainly private), unlike Beveridge where both are public, and Bismarck where multiple sickness funds exist.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: Which of the following is a correct statement about out-of-pocket (OOP) health expenditure in India?
o: OOP spending has historically been the single largest source of health financing in India, pushing many households into poverty each year
OOP spending is negligible because of government hospitals
OOP spending is mostly on in-patient care in public hospitals
OOP spending is fully reimbursed through Section 80D
e: National Health Accounts show OOP as the largest component of total health expenditure, though its share has declined below 50% in recent years; Section 80D only gives a tax deduction.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: The National Health Policy, 2017 set a target of raising public health expenditure to what share of GDP?
e: NHP 2017 targets public health spending of 2.5% of GDP by 2025, up from around 1.2–1.5% at the time.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY identifies beneficiary families primarily on the basis of:
o: Deprivation and occupational criteria from the Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) 2011 data, with State additions
Income tax returns
Ration card colour alone
Health insurance history
e: PM-JAY uses SECC 2011 deprivation criteria (rural) and occupational categories (urban), and States may extend coverage; in 2024 all citizens aged 70 and above were added regardless of income.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: Under the ESI Scheme, the rates of contribution as a percentage of wages are:
o: Employee 1.75%, employer 4.75%
Employee 0.75%, employer 3.25%
Employee 1%, employer 3%
Employee 2%, employer 2%
e: Contribution rates were reduced to 0.75% (employee) and 3.25% (employer) from July 2019; the earlier rates were 1.75% and 4.75%.

t: Under the 2024 Master Circular on health insurance, an insurer must decide on a cashless pre-authorisation request within:
o: 1 hour
30 minutes
3 hours
6 hours
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Cashless authorisation must be decided within 1 hour of the request and final discharge authorisation within 3 hours; delay beyond 3 hours makes any extra hospital charges the insurer's cost.

t: 'Co-payment' in a health insurance policy means:
o: The insurer and reinsurer share each claim
Premium paid jointly by husband and wife
A fixed percentage of each admissible claim that the insured must bear, which does not reduce the sum insured
Payment made by the TPA to the hospital
e: Co-pay is the insured's share of each claim expressed as a percentage; unlike a deductible it is not a fixed amount and it is not deducted from the sum insured.

t: A health policy that is taken by an employer for employees and allows them to continue cover individually after leaving the organisation is said to offer:
o: Subrogation
Experience rating
Facultative cover
Conversion or migration rights to an individual policy
e: IRDAI requires group policyholders' members to be offered migration to an individual or floater policy with continuity credit when they leave the group.

t: Which of the following statements about a 'deductible' is correct?
o: It is a percentage of every claim borne by the insured
It is a fixed amount that the insured must bear before the insurer's liability begins, and it lowers the premium
It is always equal to the sum insured
It is paid by the insurer to the hospital
e: A deductible is a fixed threshold amount; higher deductibles reduce premium because small claims are eliminated. A percentage share is a co-pay.

t: Mrs Nair's family floater of ₹6 lakh covers herself, her husband and two children. Her husband is hospitalised with a bill of ₹4.5 lakh in May. In November her son is hospitalised with a bill of ₹2 lakh. Assuming no restoration benefit and all expenses admissible, the son's claim will be paid to the extent of:
o: ₹1.5 lakh
₹2 lakh
₹1 lakh
Nil
e: The floater sum insured of ₹6 lakh is shared; after ₹4.5 lakh is used, only ₹1.5 lakh remains for the rest of the policy year.

t: A 'long-term' health insurance policy under IRDAI norms may be issued for a term of:
o: Up to three years, with the premium fixed for the policy term
Exactly one year only
Up to ten years
Lifetime at a single premium
e: Health products may be offered for terms of one to three years; premiums are guaranteed for the term and may be paid annually or in advance with discounts.

t: The 'Saral Suraksha Bima' standard product introduced by IRDAI in 2021 is a:
o: Standard indemnity health policy
Standard personal accident policy covering death, permanent disablement and related benefits
Standard critical illness policy
Standard travel policy
e: Saral Suraksha Bima is the standard personal accident product; Arogya Sanjeevani is the standard indemnity health product.

t: Which of the following is a typical feature of a senior citizen health insurance product in India?
o: No premium is charged after age 80
Compulsory pre-acceptance medical tests at the proposer's cost in all cases
Coverage limited to accidents only
Higher co-payment, longer waiting periods and higher premiums reflecting higher morbidity
e: Senior citizen products price for higher claim frequency through co-pay and loadings; pre-policy check-up costs must be at least partly borne by the insurer when the proposal is accepted.

t: 'Morbidity' in health insurance underwriting refers to:
o: The probability of death at a given age
The incidence or prevalence of illness or injury in a population
The number of hospital beds per thousand population
The rate of lapsation of policies
e: Morbidity measures sickness, which drives health claims; mortality (probability of death) is the key measure for life insurance.

t: When a proposal is accepted after a pre-policy medical examination, IRDAI norms require that the cost of the examination be:
o: Borne at least 50% by the insurer
Borne fully by the proposer in all cases
Borne by the TPA
Refunded by the hospital
e: Insurers must bear at least 50% of the cost of pre-insurance medical tests when the proposal is accepted; if declined, the cost may fall on the proposer as per the proposal terms.

t: A proposal form answer regarding past hospitalisation is left blank by the proposer and the insurer issues the policy without seeking clarification. Four years later a claim for the undisclosed condition arises. Which statement is correct?
o: The insurer can reject the claim because the fact was material
The policy becomes void ab initio
The claim is payable only after a fresh waiting period
Having issued the policy without raising a query on the blank answer, the insurer is generally deemed to have waived the information and cannot rely on non-disclosure
e: Courts have held that an insurer that accepts an incomplete proposal without enquiry waives the right to the information; underwriters must therefore ensure proposals are complete before acceptance.

t: Mr Arora holds a base policy of ₹3 lakh and a super top-up of ₹10 lakh with an aggregate deductible of ₹3 lakh. In one year he has three hospitalisations costing ₹2 lakh, ₹1.5 lakh and ₹2.5 lakh. How much will the super top-up pay in total?
o: ₹1.5 lakh
₹2.5 lakh
₹3 lakh
₹4 lakh
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Total claims are ₹6 lakh; a super top-up applies the deductible to aggregate annual claims, so it pays ₹6 lakh − ₹3 lakh = ₹3 lakh. An ordinary top-up would have paid nothing because no single claim exceeded ₹3 lakh.

t: Which of the following is an example of 'financial underwriting' in health insurance?
o: Reviewing the proposer's ECG report
Loading the premium for hypertension
Imposing a waiting period for hernia
Checking whether the sum insured proposed is reasonable in relation to the proposer's income and needs, particularly for benefit products
e: Financial underwriting guards against over-insurance and moral hazard in fixed-benefit covers such as hospital cash and critical illness; the other options are medical underwriting actions.

t: A proposer, when asked about tobacco use, states 'occasional'. For underwriting purposes, the most appropriate course is:
o: Obtain details of quantity, frequency and duration, as even occasional use affects morbidity rating
Treat as a non-user
Decline the proposal
Ignore the answer since tobacco is not relevant to health cover
e: Tobacco use is a significant morbidity factor; underwriters seek specifics to classify the risk correctly, rather than assuming either extreme.

t: Group health underwriting typically relies LEAST on:
o: Age profile of the group
Claims experience of the group in previous years
Individual medical examination of every member
Nature of industry and occupation
e: Groups are underwritten on aggregate parameters; individual medical examination is impractical and generally unnecessary for bona fide groups.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Under standard policy wording, 'medically necessary treatment' means treatment that is:
o: Chosen by the insured for convenience
Available only at network hospitals
Required for the medical management of the illness, prescribed by a medical practitioner, and not experimental or for convenience of the patient or doctor
Recommended by the TPA
e: The definition requires the treatment to be necessary, of appropriate intensity and duration, prescribed by a qualified practitioner and conforming to professional standards.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: 'Post-hospitalisation medical expenses' are those incurred:
o: After discharge for the same condition, within the period specified in the policy (e.g. 60 days)
Before admission for any illness
During hospitalisation for a different illness
Only at the same network hospital
e: Post-hospitalisation expenses are payable for a stated period after discharge, provided they relate to the admitted condition and the in-patient claim is accepted.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Under the 2024 framework, AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, Homeopathy) in-patient treatment must be covered:
o: Only up to 10% of sum insured
Up to the full sum insured without any sub-limit, at AYUSH hospitals meeting the standard definition
Only in government hospitals
Only for day care
e: IRDAI's 2024 Master Circular removed sub-limits on AYUSH treatment, placing it on par with allopathic treatment in qualifying AYUSH hospitals.

t: A 35-year-old proposer with no medical history applies for ₹5 lakh cover. Most insurers would:
o: Accept on the basis of the declaration in the proposal form without medical examination, as he is within the 'no medical' age and sum insured limits
Insist on full medical tests
Decline because he is self-employed
Issue only a group policy
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Insurers set age and sum insured thresholds below which healthy proposers are accepted on declaration; tests are called for beyond those limits or on adverse disclosures.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: A policy excludes 'treatment for refractive error'. Under standard exclusion Excl15, correction of eyesight is excluded if the refractive error is less than:
o: 5.0 dioptres
10 dioptres
7.5 dioptres
12 dioptres
e: Standard exclusion Excl15 excludes refractive error correction below 7.5 dioptres; higher corrections may be covered.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Mr Das has a policy with room rent limit of 1% of sum insured (SI ₹5 lakh) and ICU limit of 2% of SI. He stays 3 days in ICU at ₹12,000 per day and 4 days in a room at ₹6,000 per day. The maximum room and ICU charges payable are:
e: ICU limit = ₹10,000/day × 3 = ₹30,000; room limit = ₹5,000/day × 4 = ₹20,000; total ₹50,000 against actual ₹60,000, with proportionate deduction possibly applying to associated charges.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: 'Cumulative bonus' in a health policy is:
o: A refund of premium at the end of the year
Interest on premium paid in advance
An increase in sum insured for every claim-free year, subject to a maximum, without extra premium
A discount given for buying online
e: Cumulative bonus rewards claim-free renewal by enhancing cover; it is reduced on a claim in the same proportion in most policies.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: The office premium is built from the pure premium by adding loadings for:
o: Reinsurance recoveries and investment income
Hospital tariffs only
Claims already paid
Expenses, commission, profit margin and contingencies
e: Gross premium = risk premium plus loadings for acquisition and management expenses, profit and contingency; investment income reduces rather than adds to premium.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: A pure premium of ₹4,000 is to be loaded for expenses of 25% and profit of 5% of gross premium. The gross premium is:
e: When loadings are expressed as a percentage of gross premium, gross = pure ÷ (1 − 0.25 − 0.05) = 4,000 ÷ 0.70 = ₹5,714 (approx.).

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: 'Credibility' in health insurance pricing refers to:
o: The reputation of the insurer
The accuracy of hospital bills
The solvency margin of the insurer
The weight given to a group's own experience versus the broader book or manual rate, depending on the volume of data
e: Credibility theory blends a group's own claims experience with class rates; larger groups with more claims receive higher credibility.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) provides individuals with a unique health identifier known as:
o: Aadhaar Health Number
PAN Health ID
NHCX code
ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) number
e: ABHA is the 14-digit health ID under ABDM that links health records; NHCX is the National Health Claims Exchange for standardised claim data exchange between hospitals and insurers.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: Which of the following is a correct statement about health claims reserving?
o: Health claims have a very long tail, so IBNR is rarely needed
Reserves are not required for cashless claims
Reserves are set equal to premium received
Health claims are short-tail, but IBNR is still significant because many claims are intimated after discharge and settled in subsequent months
e: Health is short-tail compared with liability business, yet reporting and settlement lags mean a substantial IBNR provision is required at year end.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: The requirement that an insured must have an insurable interest in the person insured is satisfied in health insurance when the proposer insures:
o: A neighbour
Any person with the proposer's consent
Self, spouse, dependent children and parents
Only self
e: A person has unlimited insurable interest in his own life and health and a recognised interest in close family members; insurers generally permit cover for self, spouse, children, parents and parents-in-law.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: The solvency ratio that every insurer in India, including stand-alone health insurers, must maintain at all times is:
e: The control level of solvency prescribed by IRDAI is 150% (assets to required solvency margin); falling below triggers regulatory action.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Since 2022, health insurance products of general and health insurers are introduced under which regulatory approach?
o: Prior approval ('File and Use') for every product
No filing at all
'Use and File', where products are launched after Board approval and filed with IRDAI within a specified period
Approval by the Insurance Ombudsman
e: IRDAI extended 'Use and File' to health products in 2022, allowing faster launches subject to internal product management committee approval and subsequent filing.

t: An Insurance Ombudsman can entertain a complaint where the value of the claim, including expenses, does not exceed:
o: ₹20 lakh
₹30 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹1 crore
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). The limit was raised to ₹50 lakh by the amended Insurance Ombudsman Rules.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: The minimum paid-up capital required for registration of a Third Party Administrator under IRDAI's TPA regulations is:
o: ₹1 crore
₹2 crore
₹4 crore
₹10 crore
e: TPAs must have a minimum paid-up capital of ₹4 crore and maintain a minimum net worth of ₹1 crore at all times; registration is renewable every three years.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017, an insurer:
o: May exclude HIV-positive persons from all cover
Must offer free policies to HIV-positive persons
Must treat HIV as a pre-existing disease with a 10-year waiting period
Cannot deny health insurance on the ground of HIV status alone; HIV/AIDS must be covered subject to underwriting on actuarial basis
e: The Act prohibits discrimination in insurance on the basis of HIV status, and IRDAI's standard exclusions removed HIV/AIDS from permissible exclusions.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under Section 80D of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the maximum deduction for health insurance premium paid by an individual below 60 for self and family (excluding parents) is:
e: The limit is ₹25,000 (₹50,000 if the individual or spouse is a senior citizen), inclusive of ₹5,000 for preventive health check-up; a further ₹25,000/₹50,000 is available for parents.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Which of the following statements regarding cancellation of a health policy is correct under IRDAI norms?
o: The insurer may cancel the policy at any time with 15 days' notice

The policyholder may cancel at any time with 7 days' notice and receive a refund of premium for the unexpired period (proportionate if no claim), while the insurer may cancel only for established fraud or misrepresentation
Neither party may cancel once the policy is issued
The insurer may cancel if a claim is made in the first year
e: The 2024 norms allow policyholder-initiated cancellation with pro-rata refund if no claim has been made, while insurer cancellation is restricted to fraud or material non-disclosure.

t: The typical claim process for a cashless hospitalisation at a network hospital begins with:
o: A pre-authorisation request sent by the hospital to the insurer/TPA with the treating doctor's details and estimate
Payment of the full bill by the insured
Filing a complaint with the Ombudsman
Submission of discharge summary
e: Pre-authorisation is the first step in cashless; the insurer or TPA evaluates coverage and approves an initial amount, with final settlement at discharge.

t: Which of the following is a correct statement about settlement of reimbursement claims under IRDAI's policyholder protection norms?
o: The insurer may ask for documents in instalments without limit
Claims can be rejected by the TPA directly
The insurer must call for all required documents at one time and not raise piecemeal queries, and settle or reject within the stipulated timeline after the last necessary document
Reimbursement claims need not be acknowledged
e: Regulations require a single, complete requirement list and time-bound settlement; piecemeal queries are a recognised service failure.

t: The IRDAI portal through which a policyholder can escalate an unresolved grievance against an insurer is:
o: Bima Sugam
Bima Bharosa
Bima Vahak
Bima Vistaar
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Bima Bharosa (formerly IGMS) is the grievance portal; Bima Sugam is the marketplace, Bima Vahak the women-led distribution channel and Bima Vistaar the combined rural product.

t: In case of death of a patient during hospitalisation under a cashless claim, the 2024 Master Circular requires the insurer to:
o: Wait for the legal heir certificate before any action
Immediately attend to the claim request so that the mortal remains are released from the hospital without delay
Reject the cashless request and ask for reimbursement
Refer the case to the Ombudsman
e: IRDAI specifically directs insurers to process such requests at once so that families are not made to wait for release of the body over settlement formalities.

t: 'Grievance' as defined in IRDAI's policyholder protection framework is:
o: Any request for information about a product
An expression of dissatisfaction about an action or lack of action, or the standard of service of an insurer or intermediary
A claim under a policy
A request for a duplicate policy copy
e: A grievance is a complaint about service or conduct; simple enquiries or requests do not qualify as grievances for the redressal timelines.

t: IRDAI's Insurance Fraud Monitoring Framework requires every insurer to:
o: Appoint an external detective agency
Lay down an anti-fraud policy approved by its Board, with procedures for detection, investigation and reporting of fraud
Reject 10% of claims every year
Share all claim data with the police
e: The 2013 framework mandates a Board-approved anti-fraud policy, fraud monitoring units and reporting to IRDAI; it does not prescribe rejection quotas.

t: Which of the following is an example of fraud by an intermediary?
o: A hospital charging for unused consumables
An agent backdating a proposal or concealing an insured's illness to secure the policy
A patient submitting duplicate bills
A reinsurer delaying recoveries
e: Intermediary fraud involves agents or brokers manipulating proposals, forging documents or misappropriating premium; the other options describe provider and policyholder conduct.

t: 'Retention' in reinsurance means:
o: The amount of risk the insurer keeps for its own account before ceding to reinsurers
The commission paid by the reinsurer
The reinsurer's share of premium
The time for which the treaty remains in force
e: Retention is the ceding insurer's own net share; it is set according to capital, risk appetite and portfolio size.

t: Under a surplus treaty, the reinsurer's share of a risk is:
o: The amount exceeding the insurer's retention, up to a stated number of 'lines'
A fixed percentage of every risk
Only losses above an agreed amount per claim
Only aggregate losses above a loss ratio
e: Surplus treaties are proportional but cede only the part of each risk above retention; quota share cedes a flat percentage and excess of loss is non-proportional.
